phonemes.desc: Open front [a], labiodental [m], open central [a]; from 天 'heaven/sky'
Alveolar tap [ɾ] between close-mid [e] and open central [a]; from 照 'to shine'
Voiceless alveolar fricative [s] plus close back unrounded [ɯ]; the final vowel is soft

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-mah-TEH-rah-soo' — the 'r' is a light tap, and the final 'u' is barely voiced.

kin.label: Japanese
kin.form: 天照 (Amaterasu), short for Amaterasu-ōmikami, 'Heaven-Illuminating Great August Deity'

kin.label: Siblings

pronunciation.note: Amaterasu is Tier 2 here: the ASCII form is identical to Hepburn romanization. Her authority is mythological and political, not phonetically distinctive.

domains.title: Sun Goddess of the High Plain
domains.subtitle: Light, Imperial Ancestry, and Cosmic Order
domains.lead: Amaterasu is the central deity of the Japanese pantheon, the sun itself made divine and the ancestral kami of the imperial house. Her realm is Takamagahara, the High Plain of Heaven. Without her light, rice cannot grow, order collapses, and the world sinks into darkness.

cards.name: Sun Sovereign
cards.desc: Ruler of Takamagahara and source of light, warmth, and agricultural fertility.

cards.name: Imperial Ancestor
cards.desc: Great-grandmother of Ninigi, who descended to earth with the regalia of rule.

cards.name: Weaver and Cultivator
cards.desc: In the Kojiki she weaves divine garments in the heavenly weaving hall.

cards.name: Withdrawal and Return
cards.desc: Her retreat into the Ama-no-Iwato cave is the primal Japanese myth of restored order.

symbols.name: Mirror (yata no kagami)

symbols.name: Cave of Heaven (Ama-no-Iwato)
symbols.meaning: The rock-door of withdrawal and return, marking cosmic crisis and renewal

symbols.name: Sun-disc
symbols.meaning: The radiant disk she embodies, often rendered as a red sun

symbols.name: Magatama beads
symbols.meaning: Curved sacred jewels associated with her and imperial legitimacy

mythology.lead: Amaterasu's mythology is told chiefly in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. It is a theology of light, legitimacy, and the restoration of order after violent disruption.

myths.title: Birth from Izanagi's Purification
myths.text: After escaping the underworld where his wife Izanami had died, Izanagi performed ritual purification (misogi) in a river. As he washed his left eye, Amaterasu was born; from his right eye came Tsukuyomi, the moon kami; and from his nose came Susanoo, the storm kami. Amaterasu was given rule over the high plain of heaven, making her the senior sibling and source of celestial order.

myths.title: The Cave of Heaven
myths.text: When Susanoo rampaged through heaven, destroying her rice-fields and terrifying her weaving-maiden, Amaterasu withdrew into the Ama-no-Iwato cave and sealed it with a great rock. The world fell into darkness. The eight hundred myriads of kami gathered and performed a raucous dance (kagura). The goddess Ame-no-Uzume danced on an overturned tub, exposing herself and making the assembly laugh. Curious, Amaterasu peeked out; a mirror was held before her, and the strong-handed Tajikarao pulled her into the light.

myths.title: The Descent of Ninigi
myths.text: Amaterasu sent her grandson Ninigi-no-mikoto to rule the terrestrial world, entrusting him with the Three Sacred Regalia: the curved jewel, the mirror, and the sword. Ninigi's great-grandson Jimmu became the first emperor of Japan, establishing the imperial house as descended from the sun.

lore.syncretism: Amaterasu absorbed and was absorbed by other solar powers. Medieval honji-suijaku theory identified her as a local manifestation of the cosmic Buddha Vairocana (Dainichi Nyorai), fusing Shinto and Buddhist cosmology. State Shinto later used her cult to unify imperial ideology, and the red circle of the Japanese flag is her descendant: a solar emblem of the rising land.
lore.culturalLegacy: Amaterasu remains the most widely recognized kami in and beyond Japan. The Ise Grand Shrine, rebuilt every twenty years, is her principal dwelling. Imperial enthronement rites invoke her, and New Year shrine visits often turn toward the sun.
lore.extendedMeditation: Amaterasu teaches that light is not automatic. It can be wounded, withdrawn, and must be coaxed back by community, laughter, and courage. Her retreat is not weakness but a refusal to tolerate disorder; her return is the triumph of relational persuasion over force.

sources.name: Kojiki (birth, cave myth, descent of Ninigi)
Nihon Shoki (alternative birth and descent accounts)

lore.archaeology: The Ise Grand Shrine (Ise Jingū) is Amaterasu's preeminent cult site, rebuilt every twenty years in the shikinen-zōtai tradition since at least the 7th century CE. The Inner Shrine (Kōtai Jingū) houses the mirror, one of the Three Imperial Regalia.
